entries.title: Some Pennsylvania Democrats Are Skeptical of Washington’s Sway
entries.summary: Democrats are trying to nationalize their affordability message, bringing big names to swing districts.
entries.content:
BETHLEHEM, Pa. — Some voters in Pennsylvania think Democrats have a Washington problem.

Which is why it was a little confusing that Democrat Bob Brooks, a former firefighter backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont) and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, was hardly the main attraction at his own campaign rally Sunday.

The congressional candidate addressed roughly 150 attendees at the United Steelworkers Union Hall here. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro and then House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries followed Brooks — rather than serving as the warm-up to their featured candidate.

“I'm a little angry with the way they've inserted themselves in local races,” Ian Carlis of Upper Saucon Township told NOTUS. He said that in the Democratic primary, he’d supported Brooks’ opponent Ryan Crosswell. “Then the national people and Josh Shapiro inserted themselves in the race and turned it.”

Democrats are trying to make every competitive House race focus on affordability. The lineup at the rally illustrated a broader strategy, and one that comes with potential risks: National leaders want to have a big imprint on local elections, even as voters express skepticism over Washington’s input.

Brooks won a hotly contested primary in May for Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District and will now face Republican Rep. Ryan Mackenzie, who flipped the seat when Donald Trump was at the top of the ballot in 2024. The evenly divided district is rated a toss-up, according to The Cook Political Report.

The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee has suffered several losses in primaries it has weighed in on, underscoring some of the frustration voters have with a national thumb on the scale.

Democrats aren’t the only ones who have a Washington problem. Four current House Republicans have lost their bids for statewide office this year. Rep. Dusty Johnson, who ran for governor of South Dakota, pointed to the attacks on career politicians as a “really potent argument” that he was unable to fight against.

In Pennsylvania on Sunday, some locals came to get a sense of how in sync national politicians are with their own needs and concerns.

“It's more so like, what are the headlines they're talking about?” said Meg Kane, 42, who described her party affiliation as “frustrated.” She also wanted to know “what they think are important” and how much that aligns with what voters see as important.

Local politicians also acknowledged that their national counterparts haven't always been in lockstep with their community.

“I think that Democrats at the national level have finally realized that we need to get the economic message out, and that really resonates here locally. Some of the other social issues need to take a back seat,” Lori McFarland, chair of the Lehigh County Democratic Committee, told NOTUS.

Carmen Bell, the second vice chair of the county party, said there’s “always some massaging” that can be done to the national message.

“Regardless of what the national message is, we could talk about being a big tent, but when we get into these small communities, we have to actually listen to the people who are there and say, ‘What's resonating with you?’”

Jeffries’ message, unsurprisingly, centered on affordability. But he also made some day-one promises, 100 days out from the November midterms.

“We're going to cut down on corrupt price gouging. We're going to clean up the mess at the United States Supreme Court. And we're going to ban the president, vice president and members of Congress from trading stocks,” he said before vowing action on two additional topics that have motivated Democrats.

“We can vote for an America that keeps our promise to our cherished seniors by protecting your Social Security and your Medicare. We can vote for America when we release all of the Epstein files.”

Jeffries’ highly charged speech did get the most reaction from the audience. And Brooks said he didn't mind being the warm-up act, either.

“I was very cool with introducing,” he said.

McFarland, the local party chair, argued that it isn’t national Democrats who are hurting the party’s message.

“I think the national level has gotten that message. I don't think these democratic socialists have,” she said. “And they're the ones that I think are throwing a wrench into a coordinated, unified message because they're more worried about some of those other social issues that we all embrace, but that's not our No. 1.”

entries.title: A Player-Led Labor Effort Could Be a Sign of College Football’s Future
entries.summary: Stanford players have formed a chapter with the College Football Players Association. They hope more teams follow soon.
entries.content:
Football players at Stanford have organized a chapter with the College Football Players Association, which could be a significant first step toward athletes in the NCAA’s most lucrative sport unionizing in the future.

Others have tried, of course, and the CFBPA is not attempting to form a union at Stanford at the moment. But five years after the labor group launched, this is its first chapter led by active players, and it described the infrastructure as providing the “firm foundation for unionization and collective bargaining.” The CFBPA is hopeful the announcement Monday leads to similar organizing at other Division I football programs.

That could happen in the near future, according to Jason Stahl, the CFBPA’s executive director. The broader goal here is to give football players a real say in the decisions shaping the name, image and likeness (NIL) era of college sports. And the timing is certainly interesting, too, as a handful of U.S. senators keep pushing the Protect College Sports Act, a bill supported by the NCAA and many conferences but generally loathed by labor groups.

It’s impossible to separate any athlete organizing from what’s going on on Capitol Hill, especially with how the possibility of employment and unions plays into most — if not all — of these policy discussions. Just take it from Ernest Cooper, a redshirt senior linebacker at Stanford who was elected by his teammates as one of the leaders for their chapter with the CFBPA.

“You see what’s going on in Congress; I think it’s hard when people who can’t relate, or try to say they understand the space, are trying to govern and put rules over you when you don’t have an ambassador at that table to advocate on your behalf,” Cooper said in a phone interview. “They’re trying to determine what’s right for us without talking to us.”

Late last week, Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters he doesn’t expect a floor vote on the Protect College Sports Act before this session ends Aug. 7. And while that doesn’t mean a vote couldn’t happen post-recess, it does raise doubts about its chances of passing through the Senate — let alone the House — despite the legislation being driven by two powerful senators on opposite sides of the aisle: Maria Cantwell (D-Washington) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas).

In June, the bill made it out of the Senate’s commerce committee with a 19-9 vote. To that point, Cruz and Cantwell had a lot of control over its fate, seeing that Cruz is the committee’s chair and Cantwell its ranking member. But now the midterms are closing in. Soon, as Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Missouri), one of the bill’s co-sponsors, explained recently, focus will shift to campaigning, then to budget negotiations —- at which point the PCSA could run out of time.

A major hangup has been opposition from the SEC and Big Ten — the two biggest, richest conferences in college sports — which has led to ongoing negotiations with Cruz and Cantwell, along with Schmitt and Chris Coons (D-Delaware), the last original co-sponsor. Employment is not among the issues they are going back and forth on.

But ever since the bill was introduced, including a line about how it is “neutral on, and does nothing to alter, employee or non-employee status for student athletes,” employment has been a complicating factor for Democrats and Republicans, though largely for different reasons.

Many Republicans, in the Senate and House, want any sweeping college sports bill to bar athletes from becoming employees. That includes Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama), a former D-I football coach who’s been pushing against the PCSA, according to multiple people familiar with his messaging to fellow Republicans. This is also a long-running goal for the NCAA and its schools.

On the other side, many pro-labor Democrats believe the bill could stunt future attempts to organize college athletes. Their argument: By giving the NCAA and conferences the antitrust protection needed to regulate compensation, player movement and eligibility without the threat of lawsuits, the PCSA would set rules that should be subject to collective bargaining, like in the NFL, NBA and other pro leagues. Then to take that argument a step further: If the PCSA instituted those rules along with antitrust immunity, labor groups would lose key leverage points. Why would college athletes unionize if they couldn’t negotiate over these issues?

Which brings us back to Stanford’s new chapter with the CFBPA. On Capitol Hill, its existence should only strengthen those sentiments on both sides.

Again, it’s not an immediate attempt to unionize. But a number of factors will determine whether that’s eventually possible. One, of course, is what happens with the PCSA. Another is the outcome of Johnson vs. NCAA, a federal lawsuit that is seeking employment status for college athletes under the National Labor Relations Act. And another is whether a Democrat wins the White House in 2028, which would almost certainly lead to a more union-friendly National Labor Relations Board.

The Dartmouth men’s basketball team began its attempt to unionize when Joe Biden was president. It then withdrew its petition with the NLRB a few weeks before Donald Trump’s second inauguration.

“Collective is what you eventually want to get to, one hundred percent,” Cooper, the Stanford linebacker, said of the long-term plan for his team’s chapter and the CFBPA. “You see the NFL and how they have their players association. All I want is for college athletes to not just get what they deserve, but to be protected while playing, too.”

The CFBPA is one of a few prominent college athlete labor groups. Others include Athletes.org and the National College Players Association, whose executive director, Ramogi Huma, led the attempt to unionize Northwestern’s football team more than a decade ago. But the CFBPA, founded by Stahl, is the only group that is solely focused on football players.

While Stahl’s ultimate vision is to scale this across the country, a more specific goal is to leverage Stanford’s chapter to get more ACC teams on board. Down the line, he hopes, ACC football players would collectively bargain with the conference over compensation, player safety and so on. If that were to happen, chapter leaders from each program would participate in negotiations.

The ACC, meanwhile, has been lobbying hard for the PCSA. The conference’s Student-Athlete Advisory Committee recently sent a letter to a handful of senators stumping for the bill. When the NCAA and conferences select athletes to testify for their interests on Capitol Hill, they are usually involved with the advisory committee, which is an NCAA-sponsored program. And this letter, a full-throated endorsement of the PCSA, further illustrates the divide between the big-money sports and everyone else.

Of the 28 athletes who signed the letter, none was a football or men’s basketball player. It’s only reason one million why it’s difficult to govern D-I sports with one set of rules — and, to that end, one federal bill.

“If there is collective bargaining down the line, it would make sense for football to be the focus,” Cooper said. “It’s just where the most money is.”

entries.title: DN-Seeing Red
entries.content:
Today’s notice: DNC’s collateral. Russia sanctions split 2028 Democratic hopefuls. Both parties are hoping to land the Latino vote. Why you're still being bombarded with pharmaceutical ads. And: The “army of one” staffing the pandemic preparedness office.  

THE LATEST

Just 99 days before the midterms, the daggers are out for Democratic National Committee Chair Ken Martin, whose organization has $16 million on hand but $18 million in debt.

The scrutiny increased after NOTUS’ Elena Schneider and Jasmine Wright reported the DNC put up its headquarters near the Capitol as collateral last year to obtain a $15 million line of credit.

“After spending all of 2025 paying 2024’s bills, we are heading toward Election Day with a DNC now focused on how to pay off a mortgage on their headquarters instead of winning elections,” a DNC member told NOTUS. “Ken Martin is losing pace on a debt treadmill of his own creation. Sooner or later he’ll have to step off or be thrown off.”

The DNC has used its facility for collateral previously — including in 2019, 2018 and 2014, a DNC official said. But Democrats aren’t too pleased that their national party is in the red so close to the midterms, especially as the Republican National Committee holds $128 million in cash with no outstanding debts.

“Ken gaslighting us about the DNC’s finances and not being transparent about the financial situation makes us doubt if he can oversee the DNC during the most important primary of our lifetime,” said another DNC member.

If that weren't enough, sources told NOTUS that Martin has grown "paranoid" and is exhibiting "spiraling behavior." One incident in which sources said he threw a phone in the direction of an aide, first reported by The New York Times, isn’t helping.

Rep. Sam LicCardo (D-California) put it bluntly on X last night: “Ken Martin must resign. As Democrats, we have become too captured by failing strategies. We must fail forward, and pivot. The urgency of this moment will not reward — and our children will not forgive — torpidity.”

A DNC official pointed NOTUS to a recent Substack post in which Martin wrote that the committee has raised more money than the DNC ever has without a Democrat in the White House and said it “will be ready to win — everywhere, at every level.” Payments on the line of credit aren’t due until January.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said yesterday that he still has Martin’s back. “The chairman has my full support,” Jeffries told reporters, per NOTUS’ Kadia Goba. “We look forward to our continued partnership.”

Speaking of Jeffries, he campaigned yesterday for Democrat Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania’s 7th Congressional District, though voters there told Kadia they weren’t sure Washington’s help was welcome.

Open tabs: Republicans see ‘scary’ lack of enthusiasm among core voters ahead of midterms (WaPo); An Admiral’s Rise Reveals the Politics Driving Hegseth’s Pentagon (NYT); The shrinking world of former president Joe Biden (WaPo); Troy Jackson Will Officially Be Maine’s Democratic Senate Nominee (NOTUS)

From the campaign trail


Democratic 2028 contenders are split over the late Sen. Lindsey Graham’s Russia sanctions bill, a bipartisan move to authorize tariffs of up to 100% on the top five foreign purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas. The legislation doesn’t specify which countries could end up slapped with tariffs, a sticking point for potential White House hopefuls who want to cut into Russia’s financial lifeline but fear it hands Donald Trump too much sweeping power.

“Trump has shown himself to abuse tariff authority in a really reckless way that's causing harm to our economy,” Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) told NOTUS’ Igor Bobic.

But Sen. Ruben Gallego (D-Arizona) said helping Ukraine win is paramount: “There's been a bipartisan effort for almost a year and a half now to pass this bill, and I think that we should pass it and not let the perfect be the enemy of the good.”

Latino voters in a handful of congressional districts could determine who wins the House majority, and both parties are fighting over this key voting bloc in Arizona, California, Colorado, New Mexico and Texas. Republicans want to keep Latinos who backed Trump on their side, while Democrats are hoping some have soured on the president and will return to their column.

“We can’t be critical of people who voted for Trump,” Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, a Democrat in a tough bid for reelection in Texas’ 34th Congressional District, told NOTUS’ Daniella Diaz.

Daniel Garza, president of the Libre Initiative, a conservative Latino advocacy group, said, “We’re hearing a lot that Democrats have failed to give Latino voters something to vote for, that they’re focused more on who to vote against, and that is not good enough.”

From the administration


Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has long promised to ban drug commercials. But action toward that goal is moving slowly, NOTUS’ Paige Winfield Cunningham reports. What’s more, drugmakers are dropping more cash on the ads than they did a year ago. The top spenders? Makers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, and of drugs to treat psoriasis and Crohn’s disease.

From the states


Democrats call it honesty, while Republicans call it evidence. The 6,600 noncitizens registered to vote in New Jersey were an anomaly, and being forthright about “isolated problems” strengthens trust in the broader election system because it “demonstrates that safeguards are working,” Sen. Mark Warner (D-Virginia) told NOTUS’ Angie Orellana Hernandez.

Republicans, though, said the incident is evidence of larger election-integrity issues.

“The fact that this happened — with or without software playing a role — can neither be ignored by Congress nor dismissed as a simple, garden-variety computer glitch,” Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) posted.

NOTUS METRO

NOTUS has some of the best reporters covering D.C.-area news, sports and culture. Sign up for our local newsletter!

Local news: D.C.’s Disabled Residents Have Dismal Transit Options. Would Waymo Help? By Zara Norman

Sports desk: What the Nationals’ First Deadline Deal Really Means, by Jesse Dougherty

A Player-Led Labor Effort Could Be a Sign of College Football’s Future, by Jesse Dougherty

The LeBron James Sixers Really Could Win it All, by Martenzie Johnson

NEW ON NOTUS

Lettuce get ahead of it. Before the Trump administration dismantled it, the Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response had 15 employees. Following a string of outbreaks — most recently the lettuce-dwelling parasite that continues to sicken people across the country — the White House has re-staffed the office, but with only one health official plus a biosecurity specialist from the National Security Council, NOTUS’ Margaret Manto reports.

“That is a start, but it is not nearly enough,” one former White House official familiar with the health security functions at the preparedness office told Margaret. “You can’t run an office of pandemic preparedness and response policy as an army of one.”

More: Trump Ramps Up Threats Against Iran Despite Pause in Strikes, by Jenna Monnin

A Heritage Employee Was Caught With Drugs Trying to Get Into the Senate, Police Say, by Daniella Diaz

Trump Is Veering Toward Abandoning International Law, by Akbar Shahid Ahmed

NOT US

  • Can This Man Save Democrats? By Jonathan Martin for Politico
  • Unreleased Documentary Footage Captures Graham’s Obsessive Push for Iran War, by Josh Dawsey for The Wall Street Journal
  • Trump Seems Trapped by Iran War, Even as He Wields the World’s Biggest Hammer, by David E. Sanger for The New York Times

WEEK AHEAD

Today 

Trump travels to Michigan to speak about the economy.

The National Conference of State Legislatures meets in Chicago, with opening remarks by Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker and Oklahoma Gov. Kevin Stitt.

Tuesday 

Sen. Lindsey Graham’s funeral at the National Cathedral, with Trump delivering remarks.

Trump hosts Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the White House.

Trump hosts Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the White House.

Filing period closes for candidates running in the South Carolina special GOP Senate primary.

Special election for Georgia’s 13th Congressional District.

Wednesday

South Carolina memorial services for Graham.

The Fed announces its latest decision on interest rates.

Anthony Fauci appears before the Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee.

Thursday 

The Senate Judiciary Committee is expected to vote on Todd Blanche’s nomination to be attorney general.

Former Vice President Kamala Harris speaks at the National Bar Association’s annual convention in Nashville.

Friday

Trump holds a Cabinet meeting at Camp David.

Harris and Pete Buttigieg speak at the National Urban League’s annual conference.

Thank you for reading! If you liked this edition of the NOTUS newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If this newsletter was shared with you, please subscribe — it’s free! Have a tip? Email us at tips@notus.org. And as always, we’d love to hear your thoughts at newsletters@notus.org.

entries.title: RFK Jr.’s Big Promise to Ban Pharmaceutical Ads Is in the Slow Lane
entries.summary: Meanwhile, drugmakers are spending more on TV ads this year than last year.
entries.content:
Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has the power to stop pharmaceutical companies from advertising directly to consumers. He could do it almost instantaneously by revising the ’90s-era guidance giving drugmakers the opening to run 30-second TV ads on their products.

However, the Department of Health and Human Services is taking a different approach — one that indicates the matter is not as high on the Trump administration’s priority list as Kennedy told his supporters.

The Food and Drug Administration has posted its intent to require drugmakers to disclose all risk and safety information within ads instead of directing consumers to an external source — a way to effectively end television and radio drug ads by rendering them untenably long, experts say.

The push is through the traditional regulatory process. A senior administration official told NOTUS that the rule is “on the priority list” but there is no firm timeline to get it enacted.

“I don’t take it seriously at all,” Lars Noah, a law professor at the University of Florida who focuses on pharmaceutical regulation, said of Kennedy’s pledge to ban drug commercials.

Two days before the 2024 general election, Kennedy promised to halt the prescription drug ads millions of Americans see on their screens every day.

“Let’s get President Trump back in the White House and me to DC so we can ban pharmaceutical advertising,” he wrote on X.

Last September, President Donald Trump signed a memorandum ordering HHS to go after pharmaceutical advertising. Forcing drug companies to report all the side effects in their advertisements “might create an advertisement that’s four minutes long,” Kennedy said at the time. The FDA also sent letters to dozens of pharmaceutical companies ordering them to either halt or revise ads the agency considers misleading.

But even as Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” report last year decried drug advertising, it stopped short of calling for a ban. And Kennedy himself has spent far more time talking about his efforts to prevent chronic disease with healthy eating and exercise in speeches around the country.

Nearly a year later, the drug industry’s ad spending continues to climb.

When Americans tune into cable and network news and sports games, they are increasingly likely to see ads for medications. Since Trump’s September memorandum, drugmakers have spent $5.2 billion on TV ads, according to an analysis provided to NOTUS by iSpot, a TV measurement company. That’s 8% more than the same period the year prior.

Top spenders over the past year were makers of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs and drugs to treat psoriasis and Crohn’s disease. In February alone — the month of the Super Bowl — Novo Nordisk spent $33 million on an ad for the weight-loss drug Wegovy.

The industry fiercely opposes stricter rules on drug ads. Pharmaceutical commercials can bring in revenue five times the cost of making the ad, industry analysts say. Drugmakers, who court doctors to prescribe their medications, use commercials as a way to drive demand directly among patients.

“Clearly there is value to the companies that are buying these expensive ads, otherwise they wouldn’t do it,” Noah said.

The American Medical Association and other critics of pharmaceutical advertising say ads can mislead consumers by emphasizing the benefits of treatments while downplaying negative side effects. The consumer advocacy group Public Citizen wrote Thursday to acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas, urging the agency to ban direct-to-consumer advertising.

“The advertisements appeal to patients’ emotions, distract them, and distort their perceptions of a drug’s benefits and risks,” the letter said.

Kennedy, who believes too many Americans take medications instead of fixing their underlying health, says ads convince people they need medicines they don’t.

Such ads are confusing patients and “distorting the doctor-patient relationship” by causing people to think they need medications they don’t, the FDA notice says.

Drugmakers contend that existing regulations are sufficient.

“Direct-to-consumer advertising helps patients make informed prescription medicine decisions with their health care providers,” said Andrew Powaleny, deputy vice president of public affairs at PhRMA, the pharmaceutical industry association.

PhRMA has been lobbying against Trump’s memorandum and on a bipartisan bill from Sens. Dick Durbin (D-Illinois) and Roger Marshall (R-Kansas) that would create civil penalties for online influencers saying false or misleading things about prescription drugs, according to lobbying disclosure filings.

“If this administration is serious about wanting to address DTC advertisements, I welcome ways to work together to get it done,” Durbin said in a statement provided to NOTUS.

The United States is one of just two countries that allows direct-to-consumer drug advertising. Ad spending spiked after 1997, when the FDA issued guidance allowing companies to summarize a medication’s risks briefly enough to fit into a 30-second TV spot.

Kennedy could easily rescind that guidance, experts said, although it would almost certainly be challenged in court by drugmakers. A federal judge blocked an effort during the first Trump administration to require ads to mention the drug’s price.

“I think it is unlikely that we will see drug advertising be totally banned under the current legal framework,” said Aaron Kesselheim, a professor of medicine at Harvard Medical School.

Before entering office, however, that appeared to be a legal fight Kennedy was eager to get into.
entries.author: Paige Winfield Cunningham

entries.title: The Latino Voters in These Districts Could Decide the House Majority
entries.summary: Both parties are fighting over a handful of Latino-majority districts across five states.
entries.content:
Republicans and Democrats are fighting over Latino voters in a handful of House districts, keenly aware that they could determine who wins the House majority.

Those districts are places where President Donald Trump made significant gains in 2024, but now polling shows they are frustrated with the stagnated economy. For Democrats, that’s an opportunity to try to win back some of the constituencies they lost in 2024.

“I think we need to continue to educate and inform Latino voters of the impacts of what this administration has done, and I think there’s a lot of buyer’s remorse,” said Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, a Democrat in a tough bid for reelection in Texas’ 34th Congressional District.

“We can’t be critical of people who voted for Trump,” said Gonzalez, whose district Trump won in 2024. “We need to just have a very honest conversation that, 'Hey, a lot of us were duped and we’ve made a mistake, and we need to fix that mistake.’ And we do that by showing up this next election and vote to change the power in Congress and put the stop to some of the policies, the painful policies to Latino communities that have come out of this administration.”

The congressional districts that both parties are paying attention to span five states: Texas’ 15th, 23rd, 28th 34th and 35th; Arizona’s 6th; California’s 22nd; New Mexico’s 2nd; and Colorado’s 8th. All are seats with majority-Latino electorates, and all are considered within reach for either party depending on how voting breaks.

A spokesperson for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, Democrats’ campaign arm, said the organization is working with candidates and incumbents to make clear to Latino voters in these battleground districts that a House Democratic majority would mean change to the economy.

“The DCCC has been committed to earning the Latino vote since day one by investing early and aggressively to reach these voters. While House Republicans are focused on making life more expensive for hardworking Latino families, the DCCC is showing voters exactly how the Democratic majority will deliver for them,” Bridget Gonzalez, a spokesperson for DCCC, told NOTUS in a statement.

But some Republican candidates are betting that pocketbook issues will help them keep the Latino voters they’ve gained in recent years in their coalition.

“I believe that [high prices are] temporary, the spike that we’re seeing with the conflict we’re having in the Middle East is temporary, and to hang on, we’re going to get through it,” said Greg Cunningham, a Republican trying to unseat Democratic Rep. Gabe Vasquez in New Mexico’s 2nd Congressional District.

Cunningham, who is Hispanic, said his own background gives him an advantage in reading the mood of Latino voters in his district.

“Because I am Hispanic and because I am pretty sensitive to what’s going on here in New Mexico, I am listening and I am addressing those concerns, and I feel confident that the way that we are speaking to Hispanic voters, being Hispanic myself, and the plan that we’re putting forth really addresses those things,” he said, referencing Republicans’ agenda in Congress. “I'm not worried about a huge swing coming back the other way and going away from the Republican Party, but I am addressing and acknowledging the needs of the people here.”

Republican-aligned Latino organizers argue Democrats’ values don’t match what they see in these Latino communities.

“We’re hearing a lot that Democrats have failed to give Latino voters something to vote for, that they’re focused more on who to vote against, and that is not good enough,” said Daniel Garza, president of the Libre Initiative, a conservative Latino advocacy group.

An UnidosUS bipartisan poll from May suggested economic anxiety is the driving force behind voter sentiment, and that rising costs and inflation are shaping daily life for Hispanic families and fueling broader dissatisfaction with the country’s direction. Nearly 7 in 10 respondents (68%) said they believe the U.S. is on the wrong track, and two-thirds (66%) said Trump and congressional Republicans aren’t prioritizing economic improvement.

Garza acknowledged that Latinos across the country are disappointed with the stagnating economy and said he recognizes that the Trump administration may have played a role in that.

“I think Latinos, even though they’ve expressed certain disappointment, to be honest, with the economic results of the Trump administration thus far, I think a lot of us are seeing that Democrats ain’t offering viable pro-growth policy alternatives,” Garza said.

With control of the House hanging on a small number of seats, both parties say the races in majority-Latino districts will be decided less by national messaging than by which side does the more convincing job of showing up.

“Over the past decade, Hispanic voters have steadily moved toward the Republican Party because Republicans are earning their trust and delivering on the issues that matter most: safer neighborhoods, lower costs, lower taxes, secure borders and the opportunity to achieve the American Dream,” National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson Christian Martinez told NOTUS in a statement. “Democrats spent decades taking Latino voters for granted. Republicans are showing up, listening and earning every vote."
entries.author: Daniella Diaz

entries.title: D.C.’s Disabled Residents Have Dismal Transit Options. Would Waymo Help?
entries.summary: Advocates fear that autonomous vehicles will be allowed to operate in the District without accessibility requirements.
entries.content:
When Kelly Mack orders a wheelchair-accessible Uber or Lyft, she does so knowing that most rides will cancel on her.

Even when Claire Stanley’s rideshare is accepted, some drivers pull up to the curb, see her guide dog and tell her they don’t want her in their car.

As members of D.C.’s disability community, both Mack and Stanley are accustomed to “abysmal” experiences getting a ride. But there is a potentially powerful newcomer in the market, one that has already divided disability advocates: Waymo.

A bill before the D.C. Council would allow companies to operate a fleet of up to 200 autonomous vehicles in the District. The bill, which received a hearing this month but won’t get a vote until the fall, has its supporters, including some disabled Washingtonians who are excited by the prospect.

“There is just something very cool, as an adult who’s never been able to drive, that when you take an AV, you feel that freedom and that autonomy,” Stanley, an advocacy director at the American Council Of The Blind, told NOTUS.

But the bill doesn’t require operators to make their vehicles wheelchair-accessible, and that troubles wheelchair users, who say they have no reliable on-demand transportation service in the city.

“We support the wider disability community getting their needs met, we just want to widen the scope of what [AV operators are] required to do to meet the needs of all of our community members,” said Heidi Case, a wheelchair user and disability advocate.

In theory, D.C. residents with disabilities can use the Metro system, for-hire vehicles or the city’s paratransit service to get around. But the bus and rail aren’t door-to-door services. Rideshare is only reliable in the heart of the city and sometimes refers riders out to taxi services, which struggle with driver shortages and have limited operating hours. City paratransit has to be booked at least a day in advance, and often has multiple stops.

“They either pick you up super early, or they get you there super late, or there’s multiple people on paratransit at the same time,” Stanley said. “So, what should be a 20-minute ride suddenly is an hourlong ride.”

Mack said she and her husband once had to show up at the airport a full day before their early-morning flight because paratransit couldn’t guarantee they’d have an accessible vehicle available for her to use. WMATA did not respond to a request for comment on how it plans to improve or expand its paratransit service.

The limited options are, in part, a product of policy. D.C. green-lit Uber and Lyft’s operations over a decade ago without mandating those companies provide accessible rides. That was a “big flaw” in that legislation, Jonathan Rogers, executive director of D.C.’s Department of For-Hire Vehicles, told NOTUS. He believes District leaders have an opportunity to do something different this time around.

“Instead of just hoping that they will prioritize those issues more than [companies] did when Uber and Lyft came here over a decade ago, let’s require it,” said Rogers.

At a hearing last week, Waymo contended it can’t mandate what the automotive industry doesn’t manufacture. A Tesla spokesperson testified the company is trying to develop a “purpose-built wheelchair-accessible autonomous vehicle.”

“We are a technology company. We do not develop our own and manufacture our own vehicles,” testified Waymo spokesperson Matthew Walsh. “We have not been able to identify an electric vehicle platform that is fully wheelchair-accessible while also meeting the very unique specifications that we need to retrofit that vehicle with our technology.”

But D.C. requires taxi companies to make 20% of their fleet wheelchair-accessible. Those companies don’t employ drivers directly, and they also don’t own most of the fleet, Rogers said.

“It’s a little ironic,” he said. “It’s challenging to provide that service, but taxis are these tiny little small businesses, and they’re in the exact same position as these multinational corporations.”

Taxi companies complete about 96% of the city’s wheelchair[accessible rides, Rogers said. In 2025, taxis completed more than 166,000 wheelchair-accessible rides.

A spokesperson for Waymo told NOTUS the company is “actively assessing how we will provide an additional fleet of wheelchair accessible vehicles alongside our fully autonomous fleet,” should Waymo be allowed to operate here.

The company could do what it has done in some of the 11 cities where it operates: partner with local organizations to provide wheelchair-accessible vehicles — though with a human behind the wheel.

Private companies aren’t required by law to provide wheelchair-accessible cars, but they cannot discriminate against people with disabilities. A 2024 settlement in an ongoing disability discrimination lawsuit between the Equality Rights Center and Uber required the platform to incentivize drivers to provide wheelchair-accessible rides.

But D.C. advocates hope they will be given access to autonomous vehicles without getting tied up in court.

“I ask you to please require [Waymo] to do it,” Mack testified at the council hearing. “Otherwise, it’s putting the onus on my community to litigate.”
entries.author: Zara Norman

entries.title: The White House Is Back in the Pandemic Preparedness Game. Barely.
entries.summary: “You can’t run an Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy as an army of one,” a former White House official said.
entries.content:
Since dismantling the White House Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy, or OPPR, the Trump administration has been tested by a record-breaking measles outbreak, a cruise-ship hantavirus outbreak, an ongoing Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo and a lettuce-dwelling parasite that sickened thousands.

The White House recently staffed the office, which at its peak in 2024 had 15 employees, with just one health official, along with a second biosecurity specialist at the National Security Council. Former government health officials say that is far from where the office needs to be to effectively combat dangerous pathogens.

“That is a start, but it is not nearly enough,” said a former White House official familiar with the health security functions of the National Security Council and OPPR, who requested anonymity to speak freely about their former employer.

“You can’t run an Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response Policy as an army of one,” they continued.

OPPR was created to coordinate cross-agency responses to major public health risks. But that office has been empty since mid-2025, after all of the staffers from the Biden administration left and the health official appointed by the Trump administration to lead it, Gerald Parker, resigned.

Since then, the Trump administration has been dogged by criticism from public health experts for having a slow or inadequate response to major outbreaks.

In early July, the administration appointed Sara Brenner, a former Food and Drug Administration official, to lead OPPR, Bloomberg reported, effectively reforming the office. Another health official, Rachel Idowu, was reappointed to the National Security Council to serve as its director of bioresponse.

Former health officials say the appointments could indicate that the White House is seeking to be more involved in outbreak response.

“Sometimes it’s hard for the agencies to coordinate alone, and somebody needs to break the tie and say who’s in charge,” one former government official said.

A White House spokesperson said in an emailed statement that the the National Security Council, Homeland Security Council and Domestic Policy Council are “together handling pandemic preparedness functions to fully account for the global and domestic needs in close partnership with the agencies.”

“Dr. Sara Brenner is on detail from HHS to lead the Office of Pandemic Preparedness and Response in order to assist with the White House’s response to the multiple ongoing outbreaks,” the spokesperson wrote.

Two former health officials told NOTUS that Idowu and Brenner were experienced and well positioned to strengthen the administration’s pandemic policy and response.

Idowu in particular, they said, indicated that the administration wants to strengthen its response to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in Congo, which has exploded in case counts and is on track to be the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded. Idowu, a career epidemiologist with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, was heavily involved in the response to the 2014 Ebola outbreak.

“Truly the right person to have in that office. She can do the work of two or three,” one health official said of Idowu.

Even so, former officials said that wasn’t enough.

“There is a tremendous amount of work to be done,” Bryon Cohen, a former adviser to OPPR, said in an email. He added that Idowu and Brenner are two “very experienced, capable people” to lead pandemic preparedness activities.

“Those two individuals only have so much time in the day, and they deserve a full staff to help them carry out their mission,” Cohen said.

“What they’ll have to do is be very selective in terms of what they prioritize,” the first former health official said.

Under the previous administration, a large part of the office’s job was putting together a playbook on how to respond to outbreaks. That playbook was transferred to the National Security Council last year when OPPR was closing up shop — though it’s not clear if the Trump administration has made use of it since.

“I do think they have pulled it out. I don’t know how they’re following it, necessarily,” the second former official said. They expected Idowu and Brenner to take advantage of it.

Several former officials pointed out that during the Biden administration, OPPR also played an important role in getting biothreat policy out the door. Trump signed an executive order in 2025 putting a moratorium on so-called “gain-of-function” research, or infectious disease research that has the potential to create a pathogen that is more harmful to humans.

That executive order set deadlines of 90, 120 and 180 days for the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy to release modified guidelines for researchers. Those new guidelines have yet to be released.

“We’re now a year later, and those policies still have not been finished. And that’s because the people who work these issues at NSC and OSTP keep turning over,” a former government official said. “The government can't do interagency long-term preparedness policy when they don't have the people to coordinate that.”

The former official said they felt like Brenner’s appointment to OPPR signified a desire to have someone the administration could trust in the role. Brenner has publicly aligned herself with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., though she has not spoken publicly about her views on gain-of-function research.

In a statement, the White House spokesperson said the Department of Health and Human Services and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention are “prioritizing innovation and gold-standard science to ensure pandemic preparedness while also correcting course to prevent dangerous gain of function research and apply lessons learned from the damaging Biden approach of prolonged lockdowns and vaccine mandates.”

With limited staffing, all five former health officials who spoke to NOTUS said the U.S. is at risk of being underprepared for future infectious disease threats.

One used the World Cup to explain the danger.

“We are a team on the field with half of our players having been given red cards, and we're going up against the Argentinas, Spains and Brazils of the world,” they said. “Viruses and other infectious diseases and threats don't stop playing.”
entries.author: Margaret Manto

entries.title: Potential Presidential 2028 Democrats Split Over Russia Sanctions
entries.summary: Imposing new sanctions on Russia over its war in Ukraine is broadly bipartisan, but some Democrats warn President Trump will go too far with new authority.
entries.content:
A bipartisan bill aiming to penalize Moscow's war in Ukraine has exposed a fissure among potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders, some of whom worry the measure would turbocharge President Donald Trump’s power to impose tariffs and harm the economy.

The bill, titled the “Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026,” could get a vote in the Senate as early as next week. It would authorize tariffs of up to 100% on the top five foreign purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas, which is a key source of revenue for Russian President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine. The long-stalled bill gained fresh momentum after the sudden death of Sen. Lindsey Graham, its champion and original Republican sponsor.

But critics argue the legislation is written too broadly and would hand Trump unprecedented, broad authority to impose geopolitical tariffs on U.S. trading partners. They point out the legislation allows him to go even further than the second round of global tariffs he imposed on many U.S. imports last week, which could exacerbate inflation and raise prices for consumers.

“Trump has shown himself to abuse tariff authority in a really reckless way that's causing harm to our economy,” New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker said. “I know that we've been working to narrow that, so that's what I'm going to be looking at.”

The debate over the bill has extended to other Senate Democrats eyeing a run for the White House who are supportive of Ukraine and its fight for survival but also wary of voting to give Trump a blank check that could come back to bite them in a Democratic presidential primary.

“I've been fairly consistent that what is happening in Ukraine — and making sure Ukraine wins this war — is in direct national interest of the United States,” said Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego. “There's been a bipartisan effort for almost a year and a half now to pass this bill, and I think that we should pass it and not let the perfect be the enemy of the good.”

Another Arizona Democrat and potential 2028 candidate, Sen. Mark Kelly, is one of the bill’s 62 co-sponsors, and he said he’d have preferred imposing even higher tariffs on purchasers of Russian oil and gas. The original legislation would have authorized the president to impose tariffs of up to 500%, but that was reduced to attract more support in the Senate.

“They narrowed it, which was good,” added Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland), another co-sponsor.

Other Democratic senators who have been mentioned as potential 2028 Democratic contenders are taking a wait-and-see approach on the bill.

Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin said she is “still looking at,” the bill, referring to “interesting” questions about its tariff provisions.

Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff said he had questions about how to go about implementing the bill, while his fellow Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, another potential 2028 Democratic candidate, said that giving Trump additional tariff authorities would be “deeply concerning.”

“I would like to see if we can get to a better version of the bill,” Warnock said. “I certainly support the notion of checking Putin, and I'm deeply concerned about the implications of his ambitions, not only with respect to Ukraine, but where he might go next.”

Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, a member of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations who has also made moves fueling speculation about a 2028 bid, said he hasn’t yet made up his mind on the bill.

Supporters of the bill are working to address concerns about its tariff provisions. As it stands, it would give the president authority to impose sanctions on three groups of countries: top five importers of Russian oil, top five natural gas importers and top five Russia sanctions evaders. It does not specify which countries would apply specifically, which critics argue opens the door to tariffs on U.S. allies, some of whom also purchase Russian oil.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune is hoping to secure an agreement from Democrats to fast-track the bill, which requires the consent of all 100 senators. Without that, it would take the Senate days to consider the bill — time that Thune cannot spare given a laundry list of legislation and confirmations he wants to plow through before the Senate leaves town early next month for its annual August recess.

Democrats could use their leverage to demand votes on amendments in exchange for agreeing to fast-track the bill. But there’s no guarantee that Thune would agree, or that those amendments would succeed.

Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden, a supporter of sanctioning Russia who has raised objections about the bill’s tariff provisions, declined to answer when asked if he would object to speeding it along on the Senate floor.

“I'm going to continue to make the case to my colleagues that, after all of this work on something that is absolutely right and correct and the smart thing to do, doing something that is going to undermine the affordability agenda doesn't make any sense to me,” Wyden said.

Booker is hoping to see more changes before he supports the bill.

“Especially with Ukraine's increasing reach [in Russia], it's really time to do everything we can to support them,” he said. “But the details are really important to me.”

entries.title: On the Docket
entries.content:
Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Judicial nominations, Waymo and a new pitcher for the Nats.

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

THE LATEST

Judging by the facts, it looks like the Senate is about to help D.C.

The upper chamber is soon expected to approve the nominations of six judges for D.C. Superior Court and two for the D.C. Court of Appeals. The nominations moved out of committee last week, and are expected to be voted on before the Senate heads to recess at the end of next week.

Judicial nominations — or the lack thereof — have long been a point of contention between Congress and the District. While Superior Court and the Court of Appeals function as the city’s judiciary, their judges are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate. The process has been historically sluggish, often sparking complaints from city and court officials about judicial vacancies.

That’s even more of a problem now, as Superior Court saw a 38.5% spike in criminal cases from 2024 to 2025, due in part to the surge of federal agents.

The Senate action will go a long way to addressing existing vacancies, says courts spokesman Doug Buchanan. He tells NOTUS that two of the nine seats on the Court of Appeals are vacant, while there are 13 vacancies — out of 62 total judgeships — in Superior Court.

“But adding judges without providing the operational workforce and infrastructure that supports them limits the effectiveness of that investment,” adds Buchanan, noting that D.C.’s courts are funded by Congress. “Justice depends on an entire system working together.”







DEEP DIVE

D.C.’s disabled residents say they don’t have a reliable form of on-demand transportation. Would Waymo help?

Opinion is split, NOTUS' Zara Norman reports. At a hearing this month, some blind and deaf residents testified that they’re excited by the possibility of autonomous vehicles in the District. But the bill that would legalize Waymo and other driverless cars in the city has no requirement that those vehicles be wheelchair accessible, sparking concerns in the community.

Waymo told NOTUS that it’s “actively assessing how we will provide an additional fleet of wheelchair accessible vehicles alongside our fully autonomous fleet,” should the company be allowed to operate in the city.

But advocates want a mandate, highlighting the fact that taxi companies in D.C. are required to make 20% of their fleet accessible.





FROM THE DISTRICT


The National Guard is moving in. The federal government will spend $292 million to house thousands of troops in apartments in D.C. over the next year, NOTUS’ Raymond Fernández reports. The contract for 2,000 “apartment-style lodging units” provided by extended-stay company Placemakr is yet another indication that Donald Trump’s deployment of the Guard is a long-term commitment — this month, its stay was officially extended through 2029.

A change to property taxes? Any D.C. homeowner knows that you pay your property taxes twice a year — in March and September. But a new bill from Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau would move D.C. to quarterly payments in an attempt to smooth out the city’s cash flow over the year. Her legislation would also allow the city to explore taxing only the value of the land that a house or building is on, or taxing the land and building at different rates. That approach, she says, could make buying and building in D.C. more attractive.





FROM MARYLAND

Montgomery County has acquired White’s Ferry in a $1.5 million deal, WTOP reports. But restarting the service, which ferried people and their vehicles across the Potomac from Poolesville to Leesburg until it shuttered in 2020, would require Virginia officials to strike a similar deal.





D.C. TRIVIA


In the U.S., D.C. residents have the highest per-capita consumption of which beverage?

  1. Coffee
  2. Wine
  3. Gin
Email us your answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout-out. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow.





SPORTS

The Nationals' first deadline trade sent infielder Curtis Mead to Boston for left-handed pitcher Connelly Early. The move felt like a clear self-assessment for the new front office and coaching staff, NOTUS' Jesse Dougherty reports.

For more analysis from Jesse, check out his AMA on r/Nationals from Friday.

LeBron James is a Philadelphia 76er. What a world. NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson writes that the one thing that may trip up this uber-talented Sixers team is its collection of egos.

What to Watch Today

MLB: Nationals vs. Blue Jays, 6:45 p.m. (MLB.TV)





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com.

The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo by Kay Nietfeld/AP.

entries.title: Trump Tells the Senate to Delay Recess Until His Voting Bill Passes
entries.summary: At least four Republican senators have signed on to the effort.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said Monday that Senate Majority Leader John Thune should keep the Senate in session until his signature voting legislation clears the upper chamber — something he’s been repeatedly told is dead on arrival.

“John Thune should not allow the United States Senate to ‘leave town’ until it passes The Save America Act or, far better still, TERMINATES THE FILIBUSTER” the president posted on Truth Social. 

Trump has been relentless in calling on the Senate to pass the Republican-backed election bill that would require people registering to vote in federal elections to show proof of U.S. citizenship.

But Thune and other Republican senators have said they simply don’t have the votes, leaving them at an impasse with the White House. While many Republicans support the bill, some — including Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Susan Collins of Maine — have voted against the measure.

Trump also said that terminating the filibuster — another no-go in the Senate — would allow it to address the “looming debt ceiling.”

Some senators have called to cancel the recess to pass the election bill.

“I hereby object to any effort to put the Senate into recess in August—at least until such time as the Senate has passed the SAVE America Act—and hereby request a roll call vote,” Sen. Mike Lee of Utah posted on X on Sunday. 

He suggested he would attempt to block the recess, which could complicate the matter but would not necessarily prevent it.

Sen. Rick Scott of Florida replied to Lee to say he supported the effort.

“I will vote to stay in session unless we have passed the SAVE America Act,” he wrote on X.

Sens. Ashley Moody of Florida and Jim Banks of Indiana similarly called for the Senate to stay in session until the SAVE Act is passed.

entries.title: New Rule Could Send Hundreds of Thousands Seeking Asylum to Immigration Courts
entries.summary: The Trump administration said the change was meant to decrease the backlog of applications.
entries.content:
The Trump administration plans to funnel potentially hundreds of thousands of asylum cases to immigration courts that are denying relief to nearly all applicants.

A Department of Homeland Security rule change announced Monday could more quickly shift asylum applications from the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services to immigration judges.

The change in how the federal government handles certain asylum petitions is meant to reduce the 1.4 million-case backlog at USCIS, according to the interim final rule going into effect Tuesday.

“For far too long the asylum system has been exploited for purposes of delay and work authorization, not legitimate claims of protection,” USCIS Director Joseph Edlow said in a news release. “America’s asylum system exists to protect individuals who genuinely fear persecution and this rule will help ensure that resources are directed to the timely adjudication of those claims instead of to those seeking to use the system as a loophole.”

USCIS asylum officers handle applications for immigrants who are not in the deportation process, while immigration judges, who are Justice Department employees, oversee cases of those actively facing removal. However, the rule change would allow USCIS to send certain applications to immigration judges without interviewing the migrants seeking asylum.

That includes applications where the migrant is barred from applying for asylum because of a one-year filing deadline or is not eligible on the merits of the claim, according to the rule.

Vanessa Dojaquez-Torres, director for US policy and advocacy for HIAS, said the international Jewish humanitarian organization worries the change would lead to more deportations with less due process. She called the number of the cases that could be moved under the rule “quite astounding.”

“This rule helps design a potential process where asylum seekers never once get to speak to any government official about their claim,” Dojaquez-Torres said. “One of our biggest concerns is that this is creating a streamline for asylum applicants to be returned back to countries where they'll be harmed.”

More than 132,000 cases a year could get transferred from USCIS to the immigration courts under the change, DHS estimates. Overall, 31% of the cases in the USCIS backlog could be affected, according to the Federal Register notice.

Asylum denials from immigration judges have soared during the second Trump administration. Immigration judges denied 62% of cases in January 2025, but they denied 94% of cases in June, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse. The speedy closure of cases has decreased the backlog within the court system, which is down to fewer than 3.2 million cases from a peak of 3.7 million in 2024, according to TRAC.

Immigrants seeking asylum have a better success rate if USCIS handles their application, according to agency data. In the fiscal year 2025, the agency denied 61% of petitions that it issued decisions for. In the first quarter of this year, the denials reached 78%.

Last week a federal judge in Massachusetts temporarily blocked USCIS from rejecting asylum applications and starting the deportation process for immigrants who fail to pay the $100 annual fee enacted in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Three days after that decision, the Board of Immigration Appeals issued a decision that asylum applications should be considered abandoned if the immigrant doesn’t pay the annual fee.

entries.title: Scammers Swindled Mike Rogers’ Senate Team Out of $16,700
entries.summary: The Republican candidate in Michigan reported the “fraudulent transaction” to federal regulators.
entries.content:
Senate candidate Mike Rogers’ joint fundraising committee got swindled this spring.

Team Rogers, a joint fundraising committee for the Michigan Republican, flagged a “fraudulent transaction” worth about $16,700 in its most recent report to the Federal Election Commission. It’s the latest in a long line of financial crimes targeting political campaigns and committees.

Alyssa Brouillet, a spokesperson for the Rogers campaign, told NOTUS the political committee had unknowingly paid a fraudulent invoice on April 21 after a vendor’s email had been hacked.

“The invoice appeared to be received in the normal course of business and was approved for payment through normal channels,” Brouillet wrote in a statement. “Unfortunately, a week later, Team Rogers was notified that the vendor's email had been hacked and that the invoice was fraudulent.”

Rogers, who is poised to face the winner of the Democratic primary between Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens, did not get the money back.
Haley.Stevens.Abdul.ElSayed (3055x2037, AR: 1.50)“Despite an immediate request from Team Rogers, the bank was unable to recall the funds due to insufficient funds in the fraudulent account,” Brouillet wrote. She did not address a question from NOTUS asking if the committee had filed a police report or was taking legal action.

The lost money is a fraction of the nearly $922,000 the committee reported spending between April and June. As of June 30, Team Rogers reported raising almost $1.5 million this election cycle, most of which it splits among Rogers’ campaign and leadership PAC, the National Republican Senatorial Committee and a pro-Rogers super PAC known as GLCF Inc.

Unauthorized withdrawals from political campaigns and committees — often by trusted treasurers or advisers — have cost those groups millions of dollars since campaign finance regulators noticed an uptick in the crime two decades ago.

Sens. Chuck Schumer (D-New York), Mark Warner (D-Virginia), Tim Kaine (D-Virginia), Jerry Moran (R-Kansas), Cory Booker (D-New Jersey) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island) are among elected officials to experience recent campaign thefts.

In January, the American Fintech Council’s PAC reported losing $2,500 after “fraudulent transactions,” money it was able to recoup.

Meanwhile, two Democratic candidates accused their political consultant of embezzlement — allegations her lawyer denied when contacted by the Philadelphia Inquirer in March.

In March, federal prosecutors charged a campaign treasurer of taking a combined $200,000 from two clients — a Maryland state delegate campaign and a community organization — to refinance a loan on his yacht.

And in May, NOTUS reported that the daughter of the Seafarers International Union president allegedly embezzled hundreds of thousands of dollars from union-linked PACs.

entries.title: ‘I’ve Done More for You Than Your Parents’
entries.content:
Good afternoon. This is the Final NOTUS newsletter for July 27, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!







THE LATEST

Donald Trump spoke this afternoon in Michigan, touting his economic agenda and blasting former administrations for actions he said have hurt the auto industry in this key swing state.

  • “I’ve done more for you than your parents, OK? Your parents are good, I’m not gonna knock your parents, but I have been better to you than your parents,” Trump told the audience.
  • Former Michigan GOP Rep. Mike Rogers is expected to face a tough Senate race against either Rep. Haley Stevens or Abdul El-Sayed, who will debate tonight ahead of the Aug. 4 primary.
Trump thinks the Senate should delay its planned August recess until it passes the SAVE America Act, he posted on Truth Social this morning.

  • John Thune has repeatedly insisted that the voting bill doesn’t have the votes. “He’s got to get his job done. It’s fine. I have a good relationship with John Thune,” Trump told reporters later today. Trump added that he’s never thought about replacing Thune. 




THE HILL

Sen. Mitch McConnell is not yet medically cleared to return to work after his June 14 fall, he said in a press release that included a new photo of the senator.

The House Ethics Committee announced it is looking into Rep. Lance Gooden (R-Texas), saying it would announce next steps by Nov. 9.  





THE ADMINISTRATION

Trump said the U.S. had paused strikes on Iran at Tehran’s request in a renewed attempt at diplomacy.

  • Trump told Axios that the two countries were in “very deep talks,” but threatened “very strong military action” if they don’t move quickly.  
ICE has made plans to target and detain Haitian immigrants as hundreds of thousands of Haitians prepare for their Temporary Protected Status to expire, CBS reports.

Asylum applicants could see their cases funneled directly to immigration courts following a rule change this morning, allowing USCIS officers to potentially skip interviewing those applying for asylum and instead send them to immigration judges.





THE COURTS

James Comey asked a judge Monday to dismiss the federal charges against him for posting a photo of seashells spelling out “86 47” last year.





THE STATES

The investigation of Pete Buttigeig that separated him from his twins last month stemmed from an unsubstantiated allegation from someone authorities later deemed possibly “mentally unstable,” The Washington Post reported.

entries.title: A Former Platner Aide Says Morris Katz Has ‘Main Character Energy’
entries.summary: Katz “needs to take some time for reflection and consider if he is serving the Democratic Party well,” Genevieve McDonald said.
entries.content:
Democratic strategist Morris Katz’s public mea culpa last week for his role in promoting and protecting Graham Platner didn’t sit well with at least one person familiar with the inner workings of the former candidate’s political operation.

“I don't believe him,” Genevieve McDonald, who served as the Platner campaign’s political director until resigning last October, said of Katz. “I mean, consultants shouldn't have main character energy. We have lost the plot when consultants are doing PR tours for themselves, for their own redemption, and that is what this felt like.”

Katz — one of the people most responsible for helping elevate Platner to national stardom — appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” last week, saying he now believes some of the initial revelations about Platner, including his online history, should have been enough to end his Senate candidacy last year. Platner would go on to win the Democratic Senate primary in June, only to be forced out of the race weeks later after he was accused of sexual assault.

It was a notable admission from Katz, a rising star in his own right after helping mastermind New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s winning race in 2025.

But it rang hollow to McDonald, who said Democratic voters were robbed of a real primary because top members of Platner’s campaign dismissed the seriousness of the candidate’s actions and failed to properly vet rumors of other potential misdeeds.

“I appreciate the recognition that those things should have been enough,” McDonald told NOTUS in an interview on Monday. “However, they weren't enough in the moment, and so it doesn't repair the damage.”

Katz’s admission that he misjudged the situation is an effort to protect his career rather than a genuine admission of wrongdoing, she said, and another chance for him to build out a political status that she thinks has a tendency to overshadow his actual political clients.

“We've gotten to a point where it seems as though I've read as much about Morris Katz as I have about the candidates that he works for,” she said.

Katz and McDonald have publicly tussled before over the former political director’s decision to talk to The Wall Street Journal about allegations that Platner had sexted multiple women while he was married. During last week’s interview, Klein asked Katz whether he owed McDonald an apology, which he declined to give.

Katz’s response angered McDonald, who says he and his company, the Fight Agency, have tried to disparage her and her professional reputation since she resigned last year.

“I don’t need an apology from Morris Katz,” McDonald said. “I think Morris Katz needs to take some time for reflection and consider if he is serving the Democratic Party well.”

McDonald’s remarks mark a continuation of one of the most damaging controversies in recent party history, one that forced Democrats to pick a new nominee only this past weekend against Republican Sen. Susan Collins. Platner’s eventual decision to leave the race also led to a round of finger-pointing at some of the officials who worked for him and for months defended him vigorously from criticism.

“I do think the process was irresponsible,” McDonald said. “You know, it appears Fight Agency and Daniel Moraff were so eager to launch him and push out any potential competitors in the primary that they did not do their due diligence.”

Katz declined to comment for this story. Katz said in the interview with Klein that Fight Agency “is not a vetting agency,” but that it’d be “fair” to critique him and the firm for “putting more pressure on people to ensure that the vetting process taking place is responsible and robust.”

McDonald said she just hopes that everyone can move on.

“The past several months have been deeply challenging to me, both, you know, personally and professionally,” she said. “I'm very much ready for the nation to move on from the Platner campaign.”
