entries.title: James Comey Filed a Motion to 86 his ‘86 47’ Criminal Charges
entries.summary: Attorneys for President Donald Trump’s longtime foe say the seashell-based social media post lacked “a true threat.”
entries.content:
Former FBI Director James Comey asked a judge to dismiss a federal indictment against him Monday, arguing that posting a photo last year of seashells spelling out “86 47” did not constitute a “true threat” against President Donald Trump.

In a court filing, Comey’s attorneys argue that “86 47” is a well-known political slogan that expresses opposition to Trump, and was commonly displayed at protests ahead of Comey’s post, with thousands of items featuring the slogan sold on the internet that are available to this day.

“But the government now singles out Mr. Comey to prosecute one of the President’s most prominent critics for publishing another person’s statement of political opposition,” the filing states.

“To justify this prosecution, the indictment alleges that Mr. Comey’s ‘86 47’ post constitutes a ‘true threat’ on the President’s life,” the filing states. “That claim is contradicted by every possible source of meaning: dictionaries, context, precedent, and common sense. ‘86’ simply means ‘get rid of’ or ‘eject’ and has no violent connotation except in the most uncommon usages.”

“Most dictionaries do not even list the meaning—’to kill’—that the government now proposes,” the filing says.

Comey’s lawyers also argue the indictment “targets protected speech at the heart of the First Amendment.” And forcing Comey to stand trial would itself be a punishment of free speech that would “invite future prosecutions by the Executive Branch against perceived political enemies for their opposition to the President,” they wrote.

A federal grand jury indicted Comey in April with making threats to harm Trump. The Justice Department claimed that Comey knowingly and willfully made a “threat to take the life of, and to inflict bodily harm upon the President of the United States.” Comey was also charged with disregarding a “substantial risk that his communication would be viewed as threatening violence.”

If Comey’s motion prevails, it will be the second case against the former FBI director that has been dismissed.

A federal judge threw out a separate case against Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James in November after concluding that a Trump ally, interim US Attorney Lindsey Halligan, was illegally appointed to the role without Senate confirmation. The Justice Department appealed Halligan’s dismissal in the case.

Former President Barack Obama appointed Comey to lead the FBI in 2013, but Trump dismissed him from the post in 2017. In a two-and-a-half page memo, then-Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein cited Comey’s “handling of the conclusion of the investigation of Secretary [Hillary] Clinton’s emails.” Comey ultimately did not recommend any charges for Clinton.

While Comey was FBI director, he also handled an investigation into the Trump campaign’s ties to Russia, which the president later cited as a factor in his decision to fire Comey.

Special Counsel Robert Mueller took over the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election, and ultimately found that Trump did not commit obstruction of justice by firing Comey.

Trump has frequently referred to his longtime foe as “James ‘Dirty Cop’ Comey,” in the years since his firing and throughout the subsequent court battles.
entries.author: Jenna Monnin

entries.title: Democrats Fret Over DNC Woes but Don't Call for Martin to Go
entries.summary: Few would criticize Chair Ken Martin directly, but they said the organization’s growing problems and fundraising issues were “alarming.”
entries.content:
The internal turmoil at the Democratic National Committee has alarmed some top Democrats, who worry the national party organization is not well positioned to make gains in this year's midterms elections.

“Obviously, the amount of money they're raising is alarming,” said Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), a potential 2028 contender who has been stumping for Democratic candidates ahead of November.

The DNC has been plagued by money woes since Kamala Harris’ loss in the 2024 presidential election. The committee even put its physical headquarters in Washington, D.C., up for collateral last year in order to obtain a $15 million line of credit to help invest in off-year elections, NOTUS reported over the weekend.

Ken Martin, the chair of the DNC, is facing growing scrutiny. He was the subject of an internal human resources inquiry after throwing a cell phone in the direction of a young aide in early July, though the phone did not hit the staffer. Then there’s the promised and botched 2024 election autopsy Martin apologized for earlier this year, and many in the party blame Martin for the DNC’s paltry fundraising numbers.

Most elected Democrats are holding their fire on Martin for now, even as they acknowledge issues with the organization under his leadership.

“In a year like this, where there is such enthusiasm among rank-and-file Democratic voters and voters generally, you obviously want to have the strongest organizational footing possible, and so I'm concerned about that,” Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D-Wisconsin) told NOTUS.

Sen. Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nevada) said that she was “concerned” but believed it was “up to the DNC to decide how they want to handle.”

Potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders are so far staying mum. Representatives for Harris, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) and Rep. Ro Khanna (D-California) did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

“You know, I think they're struggling,” Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Michigan), another potential 2028 candidate, told NOTUS. “Like, Democrats have been struggling. We're still struggling. A year and a half later.”

Sen. Cory Booker (D-New Jersey), who’s also been mentioned as a possible White House contender, said Martin started the job with some “tremendous challenges.”

“He inherited a DNC that had tremendous problems,” Booker said. “He inherited a DNC that was in debt, and he inherited a party that does not have a central leader that we're all looking to.”

But Booker did draw the line at Martin’s reported treatment of the junior aide.

“You should not throw things at staff,” he said.

But the drip, drip, drip of bad news about Martin did prompt some calls for him to step aside.

“As Democrats, we have become too captured by failing strategies,” Rep. Sam Liccardo (D-California) wrote in an X post on Sunday, calling on Martin to step down from his post. “We must fail forward, and pivot. The urgency of this moment will not reward—and our children will not forgive—torpidity.”

Rufus Gifford, a former aide to President Joe Biden who served as finance director for Barack Obama's presidential reelection campaign, said that under Martin’s leadership, the DNC is “spiraling towards irrelevance,” its staff is losing faith, and there is “no saving Martin’s chairmanship.”

Shannon Watts, an author and political activist who served as a member of the DNC’s finance committee in 2024, said she has heard from frustrated donors and lawmakers who have complained about Martin.

“I've heard from very wealthy donors that they are done with the DNC and that they're sitting on donations and giving to individual candidates,” Watts told NOTUS. “And the Congress members who have reached out to me have just expressed frustration because they've brought ideas to Ken and he's just sort of strung them along and never acted on them.”
entries.author: Igor Bobic

entries.title: Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Allow New Mail-In Voting Rules
entries.summary: President Trump wants to lift a lower court ruling that blocked parts of his new regulations on mail-in voting.
entries.content:
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to allow federal agencies to move forward with new mail-in voting policies.

The application seeks to lift a lower court ruling that blocked, in nearly half of all states and the District of Columbia, two parts of an executive order from March that directed the U.S. Postal Service to create mail ballot rules and the Department of Homeland Security to compile a national database of eligible voters.

Attorneys for the administration argued that an injunction against the policies is “premature” because the agencies have not yet implemented the executive order, which gave them “substantial discretion” to do so.

“Accordingly, much remains uncertain as to what a final USPS rule might include or what the contents or uses of any DHS lists might be,” the filing says.

And, with fewer than 100 days until the midterm elections, the administration said it does not have time to let the lower court process play out first.

“Even if the agencies’ implementation plans end up being entirely lawful, there is not enough time to obtain ordinary appellate relief from the injunction in order to carry them out before the November election, especially given that any such plans will need to be implemented well before November given the timing of election procedures concerning voter-roll verification and mail voting,” the filing says.

Efforts to implement any DHS rule or USPS rule would need to begin as soon as early- to mid-August to be in place for the 2026 election, the filing argued, “particularly given that absentee and mail-in voting begin (in some States) several weeks prior to Election Day.”

The order would require USPS to regulate the redesign of mail-in ballots and envelopes. A state must also notify USPS if “it intends to allow for mail-in or absentee ballots to be transmitted by the USPS,” 90 days before the election, and any mail-in ballots submitted must be checked through a preapproved list of eligible voters.

Under the order, DHS and the Social Security Administration would develop the approved list of voters and transmit them to states to develop their “State Citizenship List.”

The president has said the new policies will help safeguard elections from noncitizen voting — though noncitizen registration is rare, according to experts.

The Trump administration’s emergency filing comes after a federal appeals court decision Saturday upheld a ruling that temporarily halted the new regulations in states that filed a lawsuit, which argued that Congress has the constitutional authority to regulate elections rather than the president.

The Supreme Court asked to hear from the states who brought the lawsuit by Aug. 3.
